newsitem.title: UK: Copper prices move ahead despite weak outlook.
newsitem.headline: Copper prices move ahead despite weak outlook.

text.p: Copper prices moved strongly higher on the London Metal exchange (LME) on Thursday, clearing important technical resistance en route to closing at the highs, traders said.
Copper rose as a less than promising long-term outlook was overlooked in favour of localised shortages of metal and the expectation of further price rises, traders said.
It was copper's apparent oversupply and abundant stocks which led many analysts to forecast a weak 1997 for the LME's flagship contract.
Traders said overall LME sentiment favoured the upside, and all markets were expected to benefit to varying degrees in the short term.
In the precious metals, however, the bearish view which has weakened gold prices by 3.5 percent since the start of the year continued.
Gold was trading at around $355 an ounce on Thursday, nearly $15 down since the start of the year and around 3-1/4 year lows. It is a rare bullion dealer or analyst who thinks the tumble is over.
"Historically, the first few days of a new year have set the tone for the first quarter, so it looks like weakness is set to continue," said a senior London bullion dealer.
But the less glamorous palladium reached its highest price in nearly four months on Russian supply concerns and prospects of rising consumer demand.
"There is a concern about Russia not being able to deliver and some consumers don't expect to receive metal," one platinum group metals analyst said.

Palladium was fixed at $122.25 per ounce, up $2.25 overnight and matching its highest fixing since September 16, 1996. It is used in hi-tech electronics applications and as part of the mix in autocatalysts which remove toxic gases from car exhaust.

LIFFE coffee futures finished $12 firmer at $1,315 a tonne after falling to a session floor of $1,280, helped by news the Brazilian government coffee auction of 120,100 bags of stocks was completely sold out, implying that the domestic market was exceptionally tight.
"We are seeing continued fund buying, it has been quite aggressive and volume again is good," said one trader.
CBOT wheat futures were lower at midsession on bearish input from the export sector and on snow in the U.S. Midwest which will help protect the U.S. winter wheat crop, traders said.

"Exports were bearish and the concern over winterkill was overblown," said Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International. At 1050 CST, wheat was four to five cents per bushel lower, with March down 4-1/2 at $3.90-1/2.
